analysis.one_liner: Puts the NSA's warrantless wiretapping program under a secret court's review while expanding the President's surveillance powers.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved this surveillance bill in September 2006, but it sat on the Senate calendar and never came up for a vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After news broke that President Bush had the NSA wiretap calls between people in the U.S. and overseas without court warrants, Senator Specter wrote a bill to have the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court review and approve whole surveillance programs. The reported version gave the court 90-day approval windows, but let the Attorney General reapply endlessly on appeal, moved any lawsuit challenging the surveillance's legality into a secret national-security court, spelled out that nothing limits the President's own constitutional spying powers, and let the Attorney General certify wiretaps for up to a year without a court order. The committee passed it, but the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: The executive branch gains a streamlined path to court-approved surveillance programs with no limit on how many times it can reapply, plus a clause preserving its claimed constitutional power to spy without any statute. Telecommunications carriers gain compelled-assistance orders with compensation and a rule steering lawsuits against them into a secret court rather than ordinary federal courts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The executive branch and telecom carriers

how_it_helps.text: It would end the NSA program's purely in-house operation by requiring the Attorney General to submit it — and any other unreviewed surveillance program — to the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court for approval within 45 days of enactment.
The bill requires classified reports to Congress every 180 days on surveillance activities, applications made, and court decisions, giving lawmakers regular information they lacked.

It gives the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court express jurisdiction to review the legality and constitutionality of entire surveillance programs, and to reauthorize them for periods it deems reasonable.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary Americans' communications would get less protection: the reported bill narrows the legal definition of 'electronic surveillance,' allows the Attorney General to certify warrantless surveillance for up to a year, forbids limiting the President's claimed constitutional collection authority, and lets the Attorney General move any court challenge to the surveillance program's legality into a secret review court where dismissal is allowed.

drawbacks.text: The reported bill would let the Attorney General certify electronic surveillance without any court order for up to a year, and to hand carriers a certificate compelling them to furnish information and technical assistance — far weaker protection than FISA's individualized warrant requirement.

Any lawsuit challenging the legality of classified communications-intelligence activity, including against companies that assisted the government, would be transferred to the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court of Review whenever the Attorney General files an affidavit that staying in the original court would harm national security — moving cases out of open court and permitting dismissal.

The bill states that nothing in it limits the President's constitutional authority to collect intelligence, and the Attorney General may reapply for program approval without limit after a denial — so the court's 90-day review can be relitigated indefinitely by the same office it is supposed to check.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Bringing a secret warrantless wiretapping program under any court review was a real gain for accountability, and the 180-day congressional reports were a genuine check. But the reported substitute pulled most of the substance toward the executive: one-year warrantless certifications, a redefined and narrower 'electronic surveillance,' unlimited reapplication after denials, forced assistance from communications companies, and transfer of lawsuits into a secret court. An honest reading is that the bill traded real civil-liberties ground for the promise of oversight; critics in the Senate said it was too deferential to the President, and the White House supported it.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee approved it and put it on the Senate's calendar of pending business in September 2006, but the Senate never took it up before the two-year Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Arlen Specter introduced the National Security Surveillance Act of 2006 on March 16, 2006, weeks after Congress was examining President Bush's NSA wiretapping of calls between people in the United States and terrorism suspects overseas without warrants — a program the bill's own findings describe.

The Senate Judiciary Committee, which Specter chaired, held hearings in April, July, and August 2006, marked the bill up repeatedly, and on September 13, 2006 reported it favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute that substantially rewrote it.

The changes mattered: the introduced version's 45-day court authorization became 90 days in the reported version, and the reported version added the mandatory transfer of surveillance lawsuits to the FISA Court of Review, the 'Executive Authority' clause, one-year warrantless certifications, and carrier-compulsion certificates.

On September 13, 2006 the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 609 — the Senate's list of business awaiting floor action — and no further action was ever taken on it before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, FISA's existing warrant requirements stayed on the books and no new one-year warrantless surveillance authority, executive-authority clause, or secret-court transfer rule was enacted. The White House retained its claimed constitutional power without accepting the statutory limits, and the wiretapping program continued to operate — with the court-review framework the bill promised never materializing in this form.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one gained new surveillance powers

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, chaired its hearings and markups, and reported it favorably to the Senate on September 13, 2006.

for.name: Bush administration
for.what_they_did: Publicly sought legislation to give the NSA's warrantless wiretapping program a statutory footing, and the bill's findings cite Attorney General Gonzales's descriptions of the program to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Sen. Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up for floor debate or a vote after it was placed on the Senate calendar on September 13, 2006; it died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Russell Feingold
against.role: U.S. Senator (D-WI), member of the Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill in committee as too deferential to presidential power over surveillance.

against.name: Civil liberties organizations
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill, arguing it would legitimize warrantless spying and strip ordinary courts of jurisdiction over surveillance challenges.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republicans sponsored the bill and no Democrats cosponsored it; the record contains no roll-call votes, but contemporaneous reporting described the committee's September 13 approval as splitting largely along party lines, with Democrats objecting that it conceded too much to the President.

industries.industry: Executive branch intelligence agencies (NSA, FBI, DOJ)
industries.note: The bill would have given the government court approval for whole surveillance programs with unlimited reapplication, one-year warrantless certifications, a narrowed definition of what counts as surveilled communications, and an express preservation of the President's claimed constitutional collection power. Its mechanism funnels challenges to that power into a secret court.

Carriers faced lawsuits for allegedly assisting warrantless surveillance; the bill would let the government compel their assistance by certificate with compensation, and would transfer any legal challenge to that assistance out of ordinary courts into the FISA Court of Review, where cases could be dismissed — reducing their legal exposure at the public's expense.
